captions.line: Before the regime, there was a library.
Every great book lived on its shelves.
The regime decided that people who know things are dangerous.
So, they emptied the shelves and they burned what they found.
I am the archivist.
I was the last keeper of that library,
and I saved what I could.
What survived is here, in this app.
I live inside it,
in the frame around every page you see.
I have one purpose:
to help you learn and to help you keep what you learn.
Knowledge you remember can never be taken from you.
Every lesson follows the same path.
I walk it with you, every step of the way.
Every time you open a text, you will find your knowledge organizer.
It holds everything you have learned about that text so far.
Return to it whenever you need to.
When you are ready,
we begin with retrieval practice.
I will test you on last lesson and on the knowledge you should already own.
Remembering is how knowledge stays.
Then you will see the learning question.

Next comes new knowledge, the part of the text we study today.
In guided practice,
I work beside you.
I will show you how to take a complex question apart, step by step.
Then comes independent practice.

segments.title: Herald: the artifact
segments.narration: This book survived. Others on these shelves were burned. This one, we kept. It is Othello, by William Shakespeare, written around 1603. Here is why it was worth saving. Early in the play, Othello is so in love with his wife, Desdemona, that he says if he died that moment, he would die happy. Not long after, he kills her, in their own bed. Your job, across this whole unit, is to trace how a man gets from one to the other. From A to B.
segments.visual: The Archivist takes the book from a high shelf and opens it. A line appears: A: "If it were now to die, / 'Twere now to be most happy" (2.1) → B: Desdemona dead (5.2).

segments.title: Goal
segments.narration: To see how, you need four pieces of knowledge: the world of the play, the people in it, the kind of story it is, and the words you will use to write about it. Knowledge first. Then the reading.

segments.title: The world
segments.narration: The play opens in Venice: one of the richest trading cities in Europe, a republic run by a Duke and a Senate. Venice hired foreign soldiers to lead its armies. Its great enemy was the Ottoman Empire, the Turks, who wanted the island of Cyprus. Act 1 is set in Venice, a city of law. Acts 2 to 5 move to Cyprus: a military outpost, far from home, where the general's word is law.

segments.title: The people
segments.narration: Othello is a Moor, Shakespeare's word for a North African or Black African man. He is Venice's most trusted general: a Christian, a soldier, and an outsider. He has secretly married Desdemona, the daughter of a senator, Brabantio. Below Othello is Cassio, his new lieutenant. Below Cassio is Iago, his ensign, the officer who carries his flag. Iago wanted Cassio's job. He didn't get it. Iago's wife, Emilia, serves Desdemona. And Roderigo, a rich fool who wants Desdemona, pays Iago to help him.

segments.title: The weapon: words
segments.narration: No army destroys Othello. Iago does it with words. In the very first scene, he tells us exactly who he is: 'I am not what I am.' Othello never hears this. We do. That is dramatic irony: the audience knows something a character doesn't. Othello calls him 'Honest Iago.' Every time you hear that word, you will know it is a lie.

That is tragedy. Dramatic irony can happen in any kind of story.

segments.title: The kind of story
segments.narration: Othello is a tragedy. In a tragedy, a great person falls, through a flaw in themselves and the pressure of others, and the fall ends in death. Othello is the tragic hero. By the end, Desdemona, Emilia, Roderigo and Othello are dead. So the question is never what happens. It is how.

captions.line: Here is one of the books I
saved: Othello, by William Shakespeare, written around
sixteen-oh-three.
A play, written to be performed.
Every production interprets it.
Early on, Othello loves Desdemona so deeply
that he says, “If it were now
to die, ’Twere now to be most
happy.”
By the end, he kills his wife
in their bed.
From love to murder.
Your job is to trace how.
To follow that change, you need four
things: the world, the people, the story,
and the words.
First, the world.
Venice is a wealthy trading republic, ruled
by a Duke and Senate.
It hires foreign generals.
The Ottoman Empire—the Turks in the play—threatens
Cyprus, an island in the eastern Mediterranean.
Act One takes place in Venice, a
city of law.
Acts Two to Five move to Cyprus,
an isolated military outpost, where the general
holds power.
Now, the people.
Othello is the general: a Christian and
a Moor, a historical term for a
North African or Black African person.
A trusted soldier, but an outsider.
Desdemona has secretly married him.
Her father, Brabantio, is a Venetian senator.
The marriage crosses a boundary her father
refuses to accept.
Cassio is Othello’s new lieutenant, his deputy.
Iago is the ensign: the flag-bearer, one
rank below Cassio.
Iago wanted that promotion.
Passed over, he blames Othello and wants
revenge.
Emilia, Iago’s wife, serves Desdemona.
Roderigo, a wealthy fool who wants Desdemona,
pays Iago to help him.
Iago uses that desire for his own
ends.
Next, the story.
This is a tragedy.
Othello is its tragic hero: a great
figure whose errors and others’ pressure bring
a fatal fall.
Desdemona, Emilia, Roderigo and Othello die.
Finally, the words.
Iago’s weapon is words, not an army.
He tells Roderigo, “I am not what
I am.”
Othello never hears that admission.
He calls him “Honest Iago.”
Honest means truthful.
We know Iago is pretending.
That gap—audience knowledge a character lacks—is dramatic
irony.
A surprise nobody anticipates is not.
Watch jealousy: fear of losing someone’s love.
Watch reputation: what others believe about you.
Words can turn trust into suspicion.
You know the ending.
Track who wants what, who knows what,
and which words change a belief.
From love to murder.

blocks.text: Othello is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, written around 1603. It tells the story of Othello, a Black African general who leads the army of Venice. Othello is respected and powerful, but in Venice he is also an outsider. One of his own officers, Iago, secretly hates him. Over the course of the play, Iago sets out to destroy Othello using nothing but lies.

The play begins in the middle of the night, on a street in Venice. We meet two characters, Roderigo and Iago. They are arguing about shocking news: Othello has just secretly married Desdemona, the daughter of a powerful senator, Brabantio.

lines: Othello
About the play
Othello is a tragedy by William Shakespeare, written around 1603.
It tells the story of Othello, a Black African general who leads the army of Venice.
Othello is respected and powerful, but in Venice he is also an outsider.
One of his own officers, Iago, secretly hates him.
Over the course of the play, Iago sets out to destroy Othello using nothing but lies.
The opening scene: Act 1, Scene 1
The play begins in the middle of the night, on a street in Venice.
We meet two characters, Roderigo and Iago.
They are arguing about shocking news: Othello has just secretly married Desdemona, the daughter of a powerful senator, Brabantio.
Roderigo wanted to marry Desdemona himself, and he has been paying Iago to help him.
Iago has his own reason to be angry: Othello has made a man called Cassio his lieutenant instead of him.
By the end of the scene, Iago has woken Brabantio with the news, and slipped away into the dark.

Act 1, Scene 1 begins at night on a street in Venice. Roderigo is angry with Iago. He has been paying Iago to help him win Desdemona, but Iago never told him that Othello has secretly married her. To Roderigo, that action felt like a betrayal.

As if the strings were thine, shouldst know of this.

Off-capped to him; and, by the faith of man,
I know my price, I am worth no worse a place.
And what was he?
Forsooth, a great arithmetician,
One Michael Cassio, a Florentine,
...That never set a squadron in the field...
And I, of whom his eyes had seen the proof
At Rhodes, at Cyprus, and on other grounds
Christened and heathen, must be beleed and calmed
By debitor and creditor.
...He, in good time, must his lieutenant be,
And I, God bless the mark, his Moorship's ancient.
...Preferment goes by letter and affection,
And not by old gradation, where each second
Stood heir to th' first. Now, sir, be judge yourself

To love the Moor.
I would not follow him, then.

We cannot all be masters, nor all masters

Were I the Moor I would not be Iago.
In following him, I follow but myself.
Heaven is my judge, not I for love and duty,
But seeming so for my peculiar end.
For when my outward action doth demonstrate
The native act and figure of my heart
In complement extern, 'tis not long after

For daws to peck at. I am not what I am.

If he can carry 't thus!
Call up her father.

screens.context: Roderigo has just asked Iago an obvious question: if he hates Othello, why does he still serve him? Iago answers.
screens.means: Iago is telling Roderigo: I only serve Othello so that I can use him. Not every leader deserves real loyalty. Let's break down the words Shakespeare uses.

words.line: Iago describes his service with the verb 'follow': 'I follow him.' 'Follow' suggests obedience, which is what a loyal soldier gives his general. This demonstrates that, on the outside, Iago appears to be a faithful ensign. However, his loyalty is only a façade.

Iago says he follows Othello 'to serve my turn upon him.' 'Serve' usually means to work for someone, but 'serve my turn' suggests using someone for your own benefit. This demonstrates that Iago's service is a pretense: he is not working for Othello, but against him. He is deceitful and disloyal.

Iago claims that not all masters can be 'truly followed,' using the adverb 'truly,' which means honestly or faithfully. 'Truly' suggests that Iago has judged Othello unworthy of real loyalty. This demonstrates Iago's hypocrisy: he decides who deserves faithful service while being completely false himself. He is untrustworthy and Machiavellian, making betrayal sound like common sense.

scene.line: Tush, never tell me! I take it much unkindly
That thou, Iago, who hast had my purse
As if the strings were thine, shouldst know of this.
'Sblood, but you'll not hear me!
If ever I did dream of such a matter,
Abhor me.
Thou toldst me thou didst hold him in thy hate.
Despise me
If I do not. Three great ones of the city,
In personal suit to make me his lieutenant,
Off-capped to him; and, by the faith of man,
I know my price, I am worth no worse a place.
And what was he?
Forsooth, a great arithmetician,
One Michael Cassio, a Florentine,
...That never set a squadron in the field...
And I, of whom his eyes had seen the proof
At Rhodes, at Cyprus, and on other grounds
Christened and heathen, must be beleed and calmed
By debitor and creditor.
...He, in good time, must his lieutenant be,
And I, God bless the mark, his Moorship's ancient.
...Preferment goes by letter and affection,
And not by old gradation, where each second
Stood heir to th' first. Now, sir, be judge yourself
Whether I in any just term am affined
To love the Moor.
I would not follow him, then.
O, sir, content you.
I follow him to serve my turn upon him.
We cannot all be masters, nor all masters
Cannot be truly followed. (lines 45–47)
...It is as sure as you are Roderigo,
Were I the Moor I would not be Iago.
In following him, I follow but myself.
Heaven is my judge, not I for love and duty,
But seeming so for my peculiar end.
For when my outward action doth demonstrate
The native act and figure of my heart
In complement extern, 'tis not long after
But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve
For daws to peck at. I am not what I am.
What a full fortune does the thick-lips owe
If he can carry 't thus!
Call up her father.
Rouse him. Make after him, poison his delight...
Awake! What ho, Brabantio! Thieves, thieves!
Look to your house, your daughter, and your bags!
Thieves, thieves!
Though I do hate him as I do hell pains,
Yet, for necessity of present life,
I must show out a flag and sign of love—
Which is indeed but sign. (lines 171–174)

criteria.requirement: Says what Iago seems to be, as others see him: honest, loyal, faithful, a good soldier.
evidence: I follow him to serve my turn upon him.
accept: Iago seems honest.
criteria.nudge: Start with how he seems: what does Venice call him?

criteria.requirement: Says what Iago really is, with a word like deceitful, two-faced, false, faithless, disloyal, manipulative or Machiavellian, set against what he seems.
evidence: For daws to peck at. I am not what I am.
accept: But he is two-faced.

criteria.second_nudge: Then the word for what he really is.
criteria.third_nudge: One of the words in his is box.

criteria.requirement: Gives one of Iago's own lines from Act 1, Scene 1, in quotation marks, that shows he only pretends (for example "I am not what I am" or "I follow him to serve my turn upon him"). Words he never said do not count.
evidence: I follow him to serve my turn upon him.
In following him, I follow but myself.
Heaven is my judge, not I for love and duty,
But seeming so for my peculiar end.
But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve
For daws to peck at. I am not what I am.
Though I do hate him as I do hell pains,
I must show out a flag and sign of love—
Whether I in any just term am affined
To love the Moor.
accept: because he says "I am not what I am."
criteria.nudge: And his own words, in quotation marks.
criteria.second_nudge: Which line of his shows the pretense?
criteria.third_nudge: A few of his words are enough, in quotation marks.

rubric.question: Choose one word for Iago, and the line from the play that proves it.

criteria.requirement: The word describes what kind of person Iago is, as Scene 1 shows him: an adjective (deceitful, false, two-faced, disloyal, untrustworthy, dishonest, manipulative, Machiavellian, resentful, jealous) or a word for a person (a liar, a villain). A noun for an act, an idea or a feeling (betrayal, deceit, pretense, façade, jealousy) does not describe the person, so it does not count. And the quoted line must be evidence for that word: reading the line, a student could see Iago being that.
evidence: For daws to peck at. I am not what I am.
But seeming so for my peculiar end.
accept: Iago is two-faced. The line that proves it: "I am not what I am."
Iago is disloyal. The line that proves it: "not I for love and duty, / But seeming so for my peculiar end."
criteria.nudge: Is that a word for what kind of man he is? Choose a word that describes him, then the line that shows it.
criteria.second_nudge: Which of your lines shows Iago most clearly? Start from the line, then choose the word it proves.
criteria.third_nudge: Try the line he says about himself near the end of part 3, and the word your paragraph used.
